title: Do Bonds Care About Fuel Prices Again?
summary:
Diesel Futures Under $4. Do Bonds Care? 

             
             
            Bonds had a solid day, but not without some help. AM gains generally aligned with a stock market swoon that briefly saw the S&P drop to multi-month lows. But when stocks bounced, bonds generally held the gains. Why might that be? Fuel prices may have the answer. Oil and diesel prices have fallen sharply so far in November. Both are back to August's levels. Diesel has been a more reliable narrator for the story of the fuel price impact on rates, and it correlated with bonds even better than stocks today.  Correlation isn't necessarily causation, but it is true that--at some point--if diesel/fuel prices fall enough, it would have a beneficial impact on inflation and the bond market.

title: Mortgage Rates Move Slightly Lower
summary: Mortgage rates fell for the second straight day with help from lower prices in oil/diesel and the stock market. These shouldn't be viewed as reliable sources of inspiration as rates often move in the opposite direction. There was simply little else to justify today's improvement and the correlations happened to line up fairly well.  While rates are indeed lower, the pace of the improvement has been slow so far this week. At 7.46%, the average top-tier 30yr fixed rate is still nearly 0.20% higher compared to the beginning of last week.  There were no big-ticket events on the economic calendar and the release of the minutes from the Fed's most recent meeting (3 weeks ago) had no impact. In general, the 2nd half of November can be fairly random for rates due to idiosyncrasies associated with the holiday trading environment.   [thirtyyearmortgagerates]

title: Bonds Cautiously Examining Stock Market Swoon
summary: Stocks hit the lowest levels in months yesterday and are heading back toward those lows in the first few minutes following the 9:30am opening bell. After yields quickly corrected higher following last week's CPI data (among other things), they've been very reluctant to follow the stock market sell-off in proportion to the correlation that existed before last week. Still, we continue to assume there's some level of weakness in stocks that would be too big for bonds to ignore. Unsurprisingly, it seems that bonds are more willing to consider this when stocks are more actively pushing into multi-month lows and failing to bounce. We can also consider some potential implied relief by the drop in diesel prices (now the biggest drop since the start of the war and only the second notable correction).
